content: 1. Feedback should be provided to stakeholders involved in the Congenital Rubella Syndrome (CRS) surveillance system. This feedback must include detailed information on the current epidemiological status of CRS, along with any necessary updates and recommendations for system improvements. 2. Rubella surveillance programs, tailored to the unique epidemiology and operational needs of a country, are critical for controlling and eliminating the disease and preventing the severe consequences of CRS. These programs involve timely disease identification, thorough case investigations, data assessments to ensure performance indicators are met, and prompt feedback to local, national, and international public health stakeholders. 3. High-quality surveillance data can identify areas where immunization programs need strengthening and where targeted vaccination activities are appropriate. In some cases, seroprevalence surveys (serosurveys) can complement surveillance activities by providing additional insights. 4. Serosurveys involve collecting serologic specimens from a population over a specified period to measure immunity status. When well-designed and properly implemented, serosurveys can provide reliable evidence about the immunity profile of the surveyed population and document progress in disease control and elimination. 5. Historically, rubella serosurveys have been conducted in various settings and populations using different methodologies. For example, in Kyrgyzstan, a serosurvey conducted after a rubella outbreak in 2001 revealed high susceptibility among women over 25 years of age. Based on this data, vaccination strategies were recommended for women under 35 years and selectively for older women planning pregnancies. 6. Serosurveys can also document susceptibility in specific cohorts, such as vaccine refusers, healthcare workers, or populations with limited access to healthcare. These surveys are particularly useful in identifying geographic areas with low vaccination coverage or large unvaccinated cohorts. 7. Rubella vaccination programs must ensure high immunity levels in both sexes to eliminate the disease. This is especially important in countries where historical vaccination strategies targeted only adolescent females to prevent CRS, leaving males susceptible to outbreaks. 8. If a country’s vaccination program did not cover individuals who are now adults, serosurveys can assess immunity levels among adults to determine the likelihood of disease circulation in this group. 9. In cases where the epidemiology of rubella indicates a shift in disease burden from children to adolescents or young adults, serosurveys can guide targeted vaccination efforts to prevent CRS. 10. When applying serosurvey findings, key questions should be addressed, such as whether additional vaccination strategies are needed, what policy actions are required, and whether further studies or efforts are necessary to achieve control and elimination goals. 11. Rubella outbreak investigations and responses vary by region and country. Basic steps include confirming the diagnosis through laboratory testing, determining if an outbreak is occurring, establishing a response team, enhancing surveillance, conducting case investigations, and implementing control measures. 12. Active rubella surveillance should include laboratory confirmation, alerting healthcare workers about the outbreak, and establishing a pregnancy registry to document outcomes such as CRS cases, fetal deaths, and congenital rubella infections. 13. Control measures depend on the country’s situation and may include ensuring healthcare workers’ immunity, implementing infection control practices, isolating contagious individuals, and vaccinating targeted groups or conducting nationwide supplementary immunization activities (SIAs). 14. CRS surveillance should be strengthened in maternity hospitals, pediatric hospitals, neonatal intensive care units, and among specialists treating infants with cardiac, hearing, or eye problems, especially in areas experiencing outbreaks. 15. A plan for preventing future rubella outbreaks should include integrated measles and rubella surveillance, CRS surveillance, routine immunization with MR vaccine, and periodic SIAs as needed. 16. Rubella-containing vaccine (RCV) is typically administered to children at 9–12 months of age alongside the measles vaccine as part of a combination vaccine (MR or MMR). In countries with a two-dose schedule, the minimum interval between doses is one month. 17. Routine RCV administration reduces the number of susceptible children, thereby lowering the risk of rubella transmission and CRS occurrence. It should be given with all doses of measles-containing vaccine as per the country’s immunization schedule. 18. RCV is not limited to young children. Teenagers and adults without documented rubella vaccination or disease history should also receive the vaccine, as rubella predominantly affects children and adolescents. 19. The vaccine is administered as a combination vaccine (MR or MMR) via subcutaneous injection after dilution with the accompanying diluent. Two doses are safe and ensure immunity in children who did not seroconvert after the first dose. 20. Many countries have introduced RCV into their national immunization schedules, often as part of a combination vaccine with measles (MR). Decisions to stop SIAs depend on factors such as vaccination coverage, rubella incidence, and surveillance system performance. 21. SIAs are complementary to routine immunization and aim to reach all children in the target age group, regardless of past immunization history. They should be carefully planned to address barriers and target high-burden areas, such as those with poor sanitation or marginalized populations. 22. SIAs provide an opportunity to deliver other health interventions, such as vitamin A supplementation, deworming tablets, and insecticide-treated bed nets, creating synergy with immunization efforts. 23. Microplanning for SIAs involves a bottom-up approach with local leaders and health officials to estimate resource needs and ensure effective implementation.
